On Robert Ledru

The Chicago detective’s historical parallel, mentioned in To All My Darlings, is Robert Ledru, a French detective of the 1880s who was celebrated for solving difficult crimes, until a murder investigation led to the discovery that he himself was the killer. An experiment established that Ledru suffered from a condition that caused him to sleepwalk and, if he had access to a weapon in that state, to kill, with no conscious memory afterward. He was the crime and the investigation simultaneously, the detective who could not solve his own case because the perpetrator was himself. Young’s Chicago detective operates in this same inverted structure, and To All My Darlings notes that Young herself considered a similar pattern for Mr. Spitzer before being advised to remove it. The detective-as-murderer is a structural obsession in the novel: truth and its violation housed in the same body.

On Mother-Blaming (Ch 76)

On Mother-Blaming

The chapter raises the cycle of cruelty: the idea that boys who kill their mothers did so “because their mothers had already killed them, in quick ways and slow ways.” Young presents this not as justification but as observation: cruelty does not originate in a single moment, blame cannot be simply assigned, patterns of harm move through bodies and generations. This is also, in its historical context, a refusal of the dominant psychological and social discourse that placed all responsibility for children’s failures on mothers. “Mother-blaming” (the practice of holding mothers primarily accountable for their children’s developmental, behavioral, and psychological outcomes) was a defining feature of mid-twentieth century psychology, from Freudian theory through the pathologizing of the “schizophrenogenic mother.” Young’s novel, which gives us Catherine’s opium dreaming and Esther’s endless stillborn and the woman in curlers and the Landlady and Tabitha, refuses this reduction. Mothers in this novel are not the cause of their children’s problems. They are people (enormous, eccentric, suffering, luminous people) inside their own impossible situations.

On Blackstone and the law firm.

Mr. Spitzer's firm is named Blackstone, after Sir William Blackstone, the eighteenth-century English jurist whose Commentaries on the Laws of England was foundational to both English and American law. That Mr. Spitzer works for a firm bearing this name is Young's quiet joke about the man who values dignity more than life: he is the heir of a legal tradition that prioritizes the protection of the innocent over the punishment of the guilty, that has built an entire system of procedure to prevent the wrong person from being convicted. The law firm that bears the name of the great protector of innocence employs a man who is not sure he is innocent of being someone else.

On eternalism and the block universe.

Eternalism is the philosophical view that all times (past, present, and future) are equally real, forming a four-dimensional block that simply exists rather than flowing. Your grandmother at twenty is as real as you are now; she is just located at a different coordinate in the block. The dead are not absent; they are present at their own temporal addresses. Young's novel does not argue for eternalism explicitly, but it inhabits its logic: Catherine's memories are as real as the present moment, Cousin Hannah's life is as present in its dying as in its triumph, and the question of whether the lid is lowering or raising becomes genuinely open when no moment is more real than any other.

On Baby Farming and Amelia Dyer

Baby farming (the practice of accepting custody of infants for payment, which in its most criminal form became cover for systematic murder) was a documented practice in Victorian Britain and, to a lesser extent, Australia and the United States. The most notorious practitioner was Amelia Dyer, who murdered infants in her care over approximately thirty years during the Victorian era. Trained as a nurse and widowed, Dyer took in infants and kept their fees while killing the children, disposing of bodies in the River Thames. She was caught when a child’s body was recovered from the river: the same method of disposal Esther uses for the mud baby. Her daughter, known as Polly, assisted her. Young’s “timid little assistant” echoes this detail. The Catholic Bon Secours Mother and Baby Home in Ireland, while not technically baby farming, represents a related institutional horror: children’s remains were later discovered in a septic tank on the property, with documented high mortality rates and abuse of mothers. These are the real histories behind the yellowed newspaper clipping the detective sends Esther.

not." This is the chapter's most compressed philosophical statement, and it deserves a moment. What Young is describing, through Mr. Spitzer, is that identity is not a fixed thing one possesses, but a dynamic one maintains by including its own opposite. To be himself, Mr. Spitzer must also be his brother, his shadow, the body that may not be his. The self is not singular. From the guide

On Wedding Rings on Nipples

One of the chapter’s strangest details: Esther wearing wedding rings on her nipples but not on her fingers. The wedding ring on the finger marks the social contract, the public commitment, the legal bond. The wedding ring on the nipple marks something private, bodily, maternal: the place where the child would be fed, where sustenance and intimacy meet. Esther has been denied the social version of love: no one has put a ring on her finger, no one has claimed her publicly, no man has stayed. But she has been married, in her body’s terms, to the act of motherhood again and again. The rings on her nipples are the marriage no one witnessed and no law recorded. They are hers alone.

From the guide

On the road not taken.

Robert Frost's poem is almost universally misread as being about the value of individuality: the speaker choosing the less-traveled road and that making all the difference. In fact the poem's speaker admits the two roads were worn about the same, that the choice was essentially arbitrary, and that the speaker is telling himself a consoling story about it in retrospect. The poem is about the stories we tell ourselves about our choices, not about the choices themselves. Young's invocation of it (“should it include the road not taken or the road taken?”) carries both readings at once: the honest admission that the roads were equivalent, and the human need to make one of them mean something more.

On the Song of Songs

Young calls Esther’s condition the “Song of Songs of the sterility which is the creation.” The Song of Songs (or Song of Solomon) is the Hebrew Bible’s erotic poem: unique in the scriptural canon for celebrating sexual love between equals, two bodies in mutual desire and delight. Commentators across centuries have allegorized it (as God’s love for Israel, as Christ’s love for the Church) but its literal text is about two people reaching toward each other. Young inverts the form: the song of sterility, the poem of what reaches toward creation and finds absence. Esther is the great erotic poem of loss. Her body is the text.

On dream logic and the logic of the opposite.

The folk tradition that dreams mean the opposite of what they show (dreaming of death means long life, dreaming of money means loss) predates Freud by millennia. Freud formalized it as the distinction between manifest and latent content, with the dream's censor disguising the true meaning in reversed or condensed form. Young gives Mr. Spitzer conscious access to this logic as a navigation tool, and it still fails him, because the tailor's shop is not accessible through any navigational method: direct or reversed. On alchemy and eternal transmutation.

The alchemical tradition sought to transmute base metals into gold, not because gold was the point, but because the transmutation was understood as a spiritual process, a refinement of matter toward its highest potential. Paracelsus, one of alchemy's great practitioners, said the goal was not material wealth but the transformation of the self through the understanding of transformation in matter. Young's use of the word transmutation for death places Cousin Hannah's dying within this tradition: not annihilation but refinement. Not ending but becoming. The lead becomes gold. The woman becomes the myth. The myth becomes the novel. The novel becomes what you are reading right now.

on-pseudocyesis-ch-77:
On Pseudocyesis (Ch 77)

From the reading guide, Chapter 77 · Research: Chapter 77

From the guide

On Pseudocyesis

Pseudocyesis, false pregnancy, is a real medical condition in which a person develops clinical signs of pregnancy, including abdominal enlargement, breast changes with secretions, delayed menstrual periods, and the felt sensation of fetal movement, without carrying a fetus. It has both physiological and psychiatric components and can be caused by physical trauma, hormonal imbalance, or intense psychological desire for or fear of pregnancy. The abortionist in the newspaper clipping kills a woman whose pregnancy is purely psychosomatic, and the impossibility of the murder, there is no baby to conceal, exposes her method. To All My Darlings notes that Esther’s own condition may be consistent with pseudocyesis, though Young never resolves this. The felt movement “of the little shadow boxer, the” two hearts, the swollen belly: all could be symptoms of a body that has been pregnant so many times and lost so much that it has learned to produce the experience of pregnancy independent of its biological preconditions. Young does not choose. The uncertainty is the truth.

From the guide

On Faneuil Hall's grasshopper weathervane.

The grasshopper weathervane atop Faneuil Hall has been a Boston landmark since 1742, commissioned by Peter Faneuil and made by the coppersmith Shem Drowne. It is four feet long and has hollow sections: used over the centuries to hide documents, including news clippings and time capsule notes, placed there during repairs. In 1974 it was stolen and recovered within days. The weathervane is one of Boston's oldest surviving objects and has become a test of local identity: if you can identify it as Faneuil Hall's symbol, you are from Boston. Young's Mr. Spitzer, navigating a Boston that keeps rearranging itself, is the kind of man who knows the grasshopper. He just cannot reliably find the building it sits on anymore.

On Irish Catholic Maids

Lisa Lunde occupies a role in the household that the novel associates with a long line of women in service: the Irish Catholic maid, the young woman who came for economic necessity and stayed because the work was there. After the Irish Famine, young Irish women, often between 15 and 24, became a cornerstone of domestic service in American cities, sending wages home, supporting families, navigating discrimination while building footholds in a country that did not entirely want them either. Lisa Lunde is not Irish, but she is in that structural position: the rational woman in an irrational household, working to support a mother who is poor and mad, carrying other people’s messages and managing other people’s chaos because her own life depends on the paycheck. Young is placing her in a long American tradition of invisible labor.

On the Blackboard Logic

The form on Mrs. Hogden’s blackboard (all a’s are b’s, all b’s are c’s, therefore all a’s are c’s) is a syllogism, the basic unit of classical deductive reasoning first formalized by Aristotle. It is logically valid: the conclusion follows necessarily from the premises. But logical validity only tells you that if the premises are true, the conclusion must be. It says nothing about whether the premises are true. Mrs. Hogden’s message uses the form of certainty to assert personal recognition. The structure is airtight. What it contains is a claim she cannot prove. “You know me.” This is what the novel keeps doing with reason: showing you the mechanism working perfectly and the product undetermined.

On oblivion as both flight and destination.

Young's observation that great people often value a moment of oblivion more than lasting glory, that oblivion is paradoxically both what they flee and what they seek, is one of the chapter's most psychologically exact formulations. The person who has given everything to a cause, who has been entirely public and entirely purposeful, sometimes longs for the relief of not being remembered, not being called upon, not being the instrument of anything. The suffragette who was ashamed of her mountain-climbing accomplishments is a person who has lived so fully in service of recognition for the cause that the private wish for invisibility has never had a moment to breathe. Young sees this. She has always seen it in Cousin Hannah: the great captain who secretly wanted the skirt, the freedom fighter who secretly wanted peace.

Marie Weed hangs herself from a peach tree because she fears another pregnancy. Young is situating this terror historically: the Comstock Laws, named for Anthony Comstock and passed in the 1870s, criminalized the distribution of contraception and information about it in the United States. Margaret Sanger challenged them publicly beginning in 1914, but full legal access to birth control for married and unmarried women in the US was not established until 1972. Marie’s death is not simply personal despair. It is the despair of a woman whose body is not legally her own.

From the guide

On sidereal time.

Sidereal time measures the rotation of the Earth relative to the fixed stars, rather than relative to the sun. A sidereal day is about four minutes shorter than a solar day: the two systems accumulate a full day's difference over the course of a year. Navigators use sidereal time to locate celestial objects; ordinary life runs on solar time. Mr. Spitzer is living on sidereal time in a solar world: his internal clock is calibrated to the fixed stars, to the long rhythms of the cosmos, while everyone around him runs on the practical daily schedule. He is perpetually four minutes off. Over the course of a life, this accumulates into a different year entirely.

On the danse macabre.

The dance of death as an artistic tradition emerged in Western Europe in the late medieval period, likely in response to the Black Death, and persisted through the Renaissance. Holbein's woodcuts are the most famous version: Death arrives for the pope, the emperor, the merchant, the child, the fool, and each one dances away. The tradition democratized death at a time when social hierarchy was supposedly eternal: a subversive gesture dressed in skeleton costume. Young reaches for it here because Cousin Hannah's death needs that tradition's frame: the great suffrage captain, for all her greatness, dances when Death asks. On the War That Makes It All Small

Esther’s closing reflection: that there is going to be another war, that it will kill “all the men and some of the children, and one or two old murders should not” matter so much: places her grief in the context of the novel’s historical setting. Young was writing across the period of World War II and its aftermath: a moment when mass death had been normalized to a degree that individual deaths (especially the deaths of women’s stillborn children, hidden in rivers, unrecorded by any official system) would be genuinely invisible against the scale of what war produced. The logic Esther uses is the logic the world used to ignore her all along: in the face of large catastrophe, small private suffering is not counted. Young does not endorse this logic. She gives it to Esther to show how thoroughly Esther has internalized the world’s accounting of her own grief, and how, even knowing this, she persists.

Benjamin Franklin did not invent daylight saving time. In 1784, serving as an envoy in Paris, he published a satirical piece in the Journal de Paris suggesting that Parisians could save a fortune in candles and lamp oil by getting out of bed earlier. He proposed changing habits, not clocks. The clock-changing idea came later, usually credited to the New Zealand entomologist George Hudson in 1895, and was adopted in the United States in 1918 as a wartime fuel measure. So Miss MacIntosh is prosecuting Franklin for a crime he did not commit, while quoting his own early-to-bed maxim back at him as evidence. Young knew exactly what she was doing. The chapter is about testimony that cannot be verified being treated as settled fact.

On the Goiter Belt

The Tavern Landlady’s goiter is not incidental. On Artificial Insemination

Young’s silver spoon is not a literal description of any medical procedure, but it sits in the historical context of early artificial insemination, which To All My Darlings documents. The first recorded case of artificial insemination was John Hunter in 1790. The first reported case using donor sperm occurred in 1884, when William Pancoast took sperm from a handsome medical student and inseminated an anesthetized woman without her knowledge or consent: a case not published until twenty-five years later. The first fertility clinic offering donor insemination in Britain was founded in the 1930s by Mary Barton, who had witnessed in colonial India how women were punished or killed for childlessness while the male partner’s infertility went unaddressed. Barton and her husband Bertold Wiesner inseminated an estimated 1500 women, with Wiesner himself fathering perhaps 600 children through the clinic, all in secrecy because the procedure was publicly condemned by both the Pope and the Archbishop of Canterbury. In vitro fertilization did not succeed in humans until 1977. Young is writing at the exact moment when the concept of medically assisted conception was real but controversial and largely secret. The silver spoon is her folkloric rendering of something that was, in the world she was writing in, happening in clinics behind closed doors, without the knowledge of the women involved, condemned by every major religious authority.

On the elegy as form.

The elegy has a long history as a poetic and musical form: in ancient Greece it was simply verse written in elegiac couplets, regardless of subject; in Latin literature it became associated with lament; by the Renaissance it was specifically the form for mourning the dead. The great elegies (Milton's Lycidas, Shelley's Adonais, Tennyson's In Memoriam) share a structure: the poem moves from grief through its processing toward some form of consolation or acceptance. Young's Mr. Spitzer has been writing his elegy for decades and has never reached the consolation. The form is right for him. He is in the grief section, permanently. On Non-Being

Esther’s closing meditation (no heart as great as non-heart, no being as beautiful as non-being) echoes a long philosophical tradition that finds in absence or negation a kind of perfection that presence can never match. The Taoist concept of wu wei, the Buddhist emphasis on the void, the Neoplatonic One that transcends being itself: all these traditions have found, in various ways, that what is not is in some sense more complete than what is, because what is must be limited and defined while what is not contains all possibilities. Young gives Esther this philosophy not as wisdom she has achieved but as the internalized lesson of a childhood that told her the non-existent twin was more real and more valued than the existing Esther. She has turned her mother’s cruelty into cosmology. It is both a way of surviving the accusation and a way of never quite escaping it.

On the Quiet Mysteries and the News Cycle

Esther’s recognition that some loud crime will break and the quiet mysteries will remain quiet forever is one of the novel’s clearest statements about how the invisible stays invisible. The American news cycle, which Young was writing against in the era of the “Big Three” television networks and the dominance of the daily newspaper, has always operated on the logic of spectacle: the loud crime displaces the quiet one, the dramatic narrative crowds out the ordinary suffering that has no narrative shape. Esther’s stillborn children are the quiet mysteries: real, real losses, recorded nowhere, attended to by no official system, of interest to no detective except the one who perpetrated the original harm. They will remain quiet forever unless she speaks, and she cannot speak in the language the courtroom requires.

On “Who Killed Cock Robin?”

The English nursery rhyme “Who Killed Cock Robin?” has been traced to the mid-eighteenth century in its written form, but is likely much older. It proceeds as a catalogue of witnesses and participants: each creature takes responsibility for some part of the robin’s death and burial. The sparrow killed him with its bow and arrow. The fly witnessed it with its little eye. The beetle made the shroud. The rook dug the grave. Everyone is implicated; no single cause is sufficient. Young gives this rhyme to Esther as a philosophical framework for making peace with the inexplicable deaths of her children: nobody killed them, and everybody did, and the forces involved are larger than any individual cause. Celtic mythology identifies Cock Robin with Lugh, the sun god who dies as the nights grow longer: a death that is seasonal, inevitable, cosmic, and always followed by return.

On Boethius and the Consolation of Philosophy.

Boethius wrote his most famous work in prison, awaiting execution on charges of conspiracy against the Ostrogothic king Theodoric. He had been a senator, a consul, a philosopher who had devoted himself to translating the Greek classics into Latin. In the cell, he wrote the Consolation of Philosophy, in which the personified figure of Philosophy visits him and argues that Fortune's wheel is always turning, that true goods are internal rather than external, that the wise person should not grieve over what Fortune has taken since Fortune gives and takes by nature. Young's Mr. Spitzer is the Boethius figure: the man of order and law who finds himself in a cell (the borderland, the liminal house) writing his own consolation, which is “that there was no threshold between world and world.”

On the World Egg

Esther’s meditations on creation (the bubble, the foam, the afterbirth, the cosmic egg) connect her to one of mythology’s oldest images. The world egg or cosmic egg appears in the cosmogonies of Hindu, Orphic, Finnish, Chinese, and many other traditions: at the beginning of everything, there is an egg, and the universe breaks from its shell. Young gives Esther this framework for thinking about her own body: the womb as cosmic egg, every pregnancy as potential creation on that scale, every stillbirth as a universe that formed and did not break through. On Mary Turner

When Vera thinks of Marie Weed hanging from the peach tree and pictures Marie’s unborn child hanging by its umbilical cord, Young is connecting Marie’s private death to a history of public racial violence. Pregnant Black women were among the victims of lynching in the United States. The most documented case is that of Mary Turner, murdered in May 1918 in Brooks County, Georgia, eight months pregnant, after she publicly denounced the lynching of her husband. The details are documented, investigated by the NAACP, and nearly impossible to read. Young does not state the connection explicitly. She places Marie’s image against this history and lets it resonate: the pregnant woman hanged, the unborn child. The private grief of a hangman’s wife contains the public horror of racial terror. Both are real. Both are part of the same American rope.

From the guide

Common sense is a real philosophical school, not just Miss MacIntosh's private religion. Aristotle named the faculty, Thomas Reid built a system on it against Hume and Descartes, Thomas Paine borrowed the phrase for the most influential political pamphlet of the eighteenth century, and G. E. Moore revived it by holding up his hand. Reid's central claim is that what everyone perceives, everyone may reasonably believe, and that the philosophers of his day had wildly overstated the gap between the world and our picture of it. Miss MacIntosh is standing squarely in that tradition when she asks who alive ever saw Caesar. What she does not seem to notice is that she is using Reid's test to dismantle her own lessons.

On the Undertaker’s Complaint

The undertaker complains that Esther brings him no business; she hides her stillborn children in streams and snow and tree stumps rather than delivering them to the graveyard where they belong, where they could be properly recorded, buried, accounted for. This complaint is comic and grotesque and also perfectly calibrated. The undertaker’s business depends on the orderly processing of death: bodies delivered, buried, recorded, charged for. Esther’s grief is disorderly. She refuses to route her children through the system. Her burials are private, dispersed, invisible, which is exactly what makes them beautiful and exactly what makes the detective suspicious. A death that is not processed by the system has not, from the system’s perspective, really been properly mourned. It has been hidden. Esther’s love for her stillborn looks, to the outside, indistinguishable from concealment of a crime.
